text: Lesson 5's COPY statement finished without an error. That's a necessary signal, but it's a weak one. A load can return successfully and still be wrong — a partition silently skipped, files picked up twice, rows dropped because of a type mismatch Redshift tolerated instead of rejecting.

None of those failure modes produce an error message. What they produce is a number that's quietly off, and nobody notices until a report looks wrong weeks later. So the fix isn't to trust the return code — it's to independently check the two sides against each other.

The curated zone in S3 and the fact_orders table in Redshift should describe exactly the same rows after a clean load. Count and sum the curated side through Athena and the Glue Catalog, completely independent of Redshift. Then count and sum the Redshift side. Line both pairs up.

After a clean load, curated_rows should equal loaded_rows, and curated_total should equal loaded_total. A row-count match alone isn't quite enough, either — it's possible for the right number of rows to land with wrong values inside them. Checking a sum alongside the count catches exactly that.

This isn't a one-time Lesson 6 exercise. The same count-and-sum comparison gets re-run in Lesson 13, right after a real nightly-load bug gets fixed, because a fix that compiles is just as weak a signal as a COPY that didn't error. Next up: a lighter-weight secondary path for querying this same curated data, through Athena.
